a3201: Course home / Phase 32 · MLOps and LLMOps in Production MLOps and LLMOps: the Production Lifecycle, Maturity Levels and Where Teams Get Stuck Lesson 32.1 50 min Lesson Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Describe the production lifecycle of a model, from data to retirement, and who owns each stage Place a team on the MLOps maturity levels (manual, pipeline automation, CI/CD automation) and pick the next step Explain what LLMOps adds to MLOps and what stays the same Before you start Needs : Lesson 2.25 · ML System Design: From Problem to Production Model ; Lesson 2.26 · Data Drift and Concept Drift: Model Monitoring in Production ; Lesson 17.13 · Choosing an LLM Observability Stack Type : Lesson (concepts with code). Time : about 50 minutes. Tools : the lessons in this phase use pandas, scikit-learn and, from lesson 32.3 , MLflow ( pip install mlflow ). Everything runs on a laptop; no GPU and no model training beyond small scikit-learn models. In plain words first The idea in one line A model in a notebook is an experiment; a model in production is a system that has to be rebuilt, tested, released, watched and retrained, and MLOps is the set of habits and tools that make that routine. The problem Most models that fail in production do not fail because the algorithm was wrong. They fail because nobody can rebuild them, nobody notices when the data changes, a "quick fix" bypasses the tests, or the person who trained the model has moved on. Google's paper on hidden technical debt in ML systems made the point with a picture: the model code is a small box in the middle of a much larger system of data collection, validation, features, serving, monitoring and configuration. This phase follows one fictional company, Lakeside Telecom , through that whole system. It has a classic ML model (predicting which customers will cancel, called churn) and an LLM application (drafting replies to support emails). By the capstone you will have taken both from a notebook to a monitored, retrainable, governed service. The lifecycle Stage What happens Typical owner Lesson Data Collect, validate, version Data engineering 32.2 , 32.5 Features Transform with point-in-time correctness, share between training and serving Data or ML engineering 32.6 Train and track Run experiments, record everything Data science 32.3 Register and approve Version the model, attach evidence, approve ML engineering, risk 32.4 , 32.13 Test and release CI tests, packaging, shadow and canary releases ML engineering 32.8 to 32.10 Serve Batch or online, with input validation Platform 32.9 Monitor Data drift, prediction drift, performance with delayed labels ML engineering, on-call 32.11 Retrain or retire Triggers, champion and challenger, decommission ML engineering, owner 32.12 Maturity levels Google Cloud's MLOps guide describes three levels. They are a useful map, not a grade to chase: many valuable models live happily at level 1. Level Name What it looks like Typical pain 0 Manual Notebooks and scripts; a model file is handed to engineers; releases a few times a year; no monitoring Training-serving skew, silent decay, nobody can retrain 1 Pipeline automation The training pipeline is code; it runs on a schedule or trigger; data and model validation; metadata tracked Changing the pipeline itself is still manual and risky 2 CI/CD automation Changes to the pipeline are built, tested and deployed automatically; registry, feature store, orchestrator Cost and complexity; only worth it with many models or frequent change Copy What you should see Copy Copy Lakeside is at level 0. The order of the gaps is the order of this phase: registry next, then validation, features, tests, release and monitoring. What LLMOps adds LLM applications keep every MLOps concern and add some of their own. The model is usually someone else's (an API), so you version prompts, model identifiers, retrieval indexes and tool definitions instead of weights. Outputs are text, so evaluation needs golden sets and graders rather than one accuracy number. Vendors update and retire models on their own schedule, so model upgrades become a routine release. Cost moves from training to every request. Lessons 32.15 to 32.19 cover these; Phase 17 already covers serving engines, gateways and inference metrics in depth. Concern Classic ML LLM application What you version Data, code, weights Prompts, model ID, retrieval index, tools, eval sets How you test Metrics on a held-out set Golden sets with graders, slices, human review What drifts Feature distributions, label relationships Question topics, document corpus, the vendor model itself Main running cost Training and serving compute Tokens per request Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Most production failures come from the system around the model, not from the algorithm. ✗ Every team should aim for MLOps level 2. Level 2 pays off with many models or frequent change; for one stable model, level 1 is often the right target. ✓ In an LLM application, prompts and model identifiers are versioned artifacts, like weights in classic ML. Recap What to keep Data, features, train, register, release, serve, monitor, retrain: each stage has an owner. Level 0 manual, level 1 automated pipeline, level 2 automated changes to the pipeline. LLMOps versions prompts, model IDs, indexes and eval sets, and treats vendor model changes as releases. Exercises Answer the ten checks for a model you know. Which three gaps would you close first, and why? Add two checks specific to LLM applications to CHECKS and justify each. Name one model where level 1 is enough, and one where level 2 is worth the cost. a3202: Course home / Phase 32 · MLOps and LLMOps in Production Reproducibility: Pinned Environments, Seeds and Content-Hashed Data Snapshots Lesson 32.2 55 min Lesson Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Make a training run repeatable: same code, same data, same environment, same result Identify a dataset by the hash of its content, the idea behind tools such as DVC Write a run manifest that lets someone else rebuild your model Before you start Needs : Lesson 0.17 · Docker Containers for AI Workloads ; Lesson 2.19 · Scikit-learn ML Pipelines Type : Lesson (build). Time : about 55 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line If you cannot rebuild a model, you cannot fix it, audit it or improve it safely; record the code version, the data fingerprint, the environment and the seeds every time. The problem Lakeside's churn model was trained eight months ago. The data scientist who built it has left. Finance asks why a large customer was flagged, and the platform team wants to upgrade scikit-learn. Nobody knows which extract of the customer table was used, and retraining "the same way" gives different scores. That is the level 0 trap. Four things to pin What How Example Code Git commit hash a41f9c2 Data Content hash of the exact snapshot, stored next to the data sha256:9e1c… Environment Locked dependencies (lock file or container image digest) scikit-learn==1.7.2 Randomness Seeds for every random source random_state=7 Fingerprinting data by content Copy What you should see Copy Copy A one-cent change produces a different fingerprint. Tools such as DVC and lakeFS store data by this kind of hash and keep a small pointer file in git, so a commit identifies both the code and the data. Seeds and the repeatable run Copy What you should see Copy Copy Same seed, same score. A different seed gives a different split and a slightly different score, which is also a reminder that a single number hides variation: compare models on the same split, or over several seeds. The run manifest Copy What you should see Copy Copy Lesson 32.3 hands this job to MLflow, which records most of the manifest automatically. The habit matters more than the tool: no model leaves a laptop without one. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A content hash changes when any value in the data changes. ✗ Setting a seed is enough to make training reproducible. You also need the same code, data snapshot and library versions. ✓ A git commit can identify the data too if the repository stores a pointer file holding the data hash. Recap What to keep Pin code, data, environment and seeds. Identify data by a content hash, not by a table name. Write a manifest with every run; let a tracking tool do it for you. Exercises Shuffle the rows of data and fingerprint it. Is the hash the same? Change fingerprint so row order does not matter, and say when that is the right choice. Train with five seeds and report the mean and range of accuracy. Add the container image digest to the manifest and explain why it is stronger than a list of package versions. a3203: Course home / Phase 32 · MLOps and LLMOps in Production Experiment Tracking with MLflow: Runs, Parameters, Metrics and Artifacts Lesson 32.3 60 min Lesson Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Record every training run with MLflow: parameters, metrics, tags, the model and the dataset fingerprint Compare runs as a table and pick a candidate with evidence Know what belongs in a run and what does not Before you start Needs : Lesson 2.18 · Hyperparameter Tuning: Grid, Random and Bayesian Search ; Lesson 2.13 · Model Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy, Precision, Recall and More Type : Lesson (build). Time : about an hour. Setup : pip install mlflow scikit-learn pandas . MLflow stores everything in a local SQLite file here; in a team, point it at a shared tracking server. In plain words first The idea in one line Every training run writes down what went in and what came out, automatically, so choosing a model is a query rather than a memory test. The problem Lakeside's data scientist tries four model types and a dozen settings over two days. The best result lives in a notebook cell that has since been re-run. Experiment tracking fixes this with one rule: if it was trained, it was logged. Setting up Copy What you should see Copy Copy Logging runs Copy What you should see Copy Copy A note on skops_trusted_types : recent MLflow versions save scikit-learn models with skops rather than pickle, because loading a pickle can run arbitrary code. Skops refuses types it cannot check, such as the tree structure inside forests and boosted trees, unless you list them as trusted. List only types you produced yourself; never trust a model file from an unknown source. Comparing runs Copy What you should see Copy Copy The runs are ranked by AUC from one query, and every row carries the data fingerprint, so you know they were compared on the same data. Close scores deserve suspicion: a difference in the third decimal on one split is not evidence (lesson 32.4 adds a proper comparison before promotion). Log it Do not log it Parameters, seed, data fingerprint, code commit Secrets, credentials, raw personal data Metrics on a fixed evaluation set, by slice Metrics on whichever split happened to be handy The model with an input example and signature Huge intermediate files nobody will open Plots that explain the model (calibration, confusion) Every print statement Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Logging the data fingerprint as a tag lets you confirm runs were compared on the same data. ✗ The run with the highest AUC should always be promoted. Small differences may be noise, and cost, latency and slices matter too. ✓ Credentials and raw personal data should never be logged to a tracking server. Recap What to keep One run per training: params, metrics, tags, model, data fingerprint. Compare runs with a query, on the same evaluation data. Keep secrets and raw personal data out of the tracker. Exercises Log the training time of each run as a metric and add it to the comparison table. Log AUC separately for month-to-month and longer contracts. Does the ranking change? Use mlflow.autolog() for one run and list what it recorded that you did not. a3204: Course home / Phase 32 · MLOps and LLMOps in Production The Model Registry: Versions, Champion and Challenger Aliases, and a Promotion Gate Lesson 32.4 60 min Lesson Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Register model versions in MLflow and point aliases such as champion and challenger at them Promote a challenger only when a gate on fresh data says it is better, by enough, on every slice that matters Roll back by moving an alias, without redeploying code Before you start Needs : Lesson 2.13 · Model Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy, Precision, Recall and More ; Lesson 2.25 · ML System Design: From Problem to Production Model Type : Lesson (build). Time : about an hour. In plain words first The idea in one line Serving code asks the registry for "the champion"; promotion and rollback become a change to one pointer, made only when the evidence says so. The problem At level 0, "deploying a model" means copying a file. Nobody knows which file is live, what evidence supported it, or how to go back. A registry gives each model a name, numbered versions, metadata, and aliases that serving code resolves at load time. Register two versions Copy What you should see Copy Copy The promotion gate The gate compares the two versions on fresh data neither was trained on , overall and by slice, and asks for a margin larger than the noise. A paired bootstrap over customers gives an interval for the difference. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Read the result before acting on it. Here the whole interval is below zero: the boosted trees are measurably worse than the simple logistic model on fresh customers, worse on the contract and month-to-month slices and level on new customers. That is a common real-world outcome when the signal is close to linear, and a good reason never to promote on enthusiasm. When the interval straddles zero, the challenger has not shown it is better, however good its point estimate looks: keep the champion and collect more labelled data. Promotion and rollback are pointer moves Copy What you should see Copy Copy Serving code that loads models:/lakeside-churn@champion picks up the change on its next reload; nothing is redeployed. Record the reason on every promotion, because an auditor will ask (lesson 32.13 ). Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Serving code should load a model by alias, not by version number. ✗ A challenger with a higher AUC point estimate on fresh data should be promoted. Only if the interval for the gain excludes zero and no important slice got worse. ✓ Rollback is moving the champion alias back to the previous version. Recap What to keep Names, versions and aliases; serving resolves the alias. Gate on fresh data: interval above zero, minimum gain, no slice worse. Promotion and rollback are alias moves with a recorded reason. Exercises Make the fresh data harder for the champion (for example, double the tickets effect in make_customers ) and rerun the gate. When does the challenger win? Add a latency check to the gate: the challenger may be at most twice as slow per 1,000 predictions. Write the alias policy for a team: who may move champion , and what evidence must be attached? a3205: Course home / Phase 32 · MLOps and LLMOps in Production Data Validation and Data Contracts: Catch Bad Data Before It Trains or Scores Lesson 32.5 60 min Lesson Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Write a data contract for a model's inputs: schema, types, ranges, allowed values, null rates and volume Validate a batch against the contract and against a reference distribution, and decide to block, warn or pass Place validation at the two points that matter: before training and before scoring Before you start Needs : Lesson 2.26 · Data Drift and Concept Drift: Model Monitoring in Production ; Lesson 2.19 · Scikit-learn ML Pipelines Type : Lesson (build). Time : about an hour. In plain words first The idea in one line Most model incidents are data incidents; check every batch against an agreed contract before a model ever sees it. The problem One Monday, Lakeside's billing system starts sending monthly in pence instead of pounds. Nothing crashes. The churn model scores every customer as high risk, the retention team phones 9,000 happy customers, and the first anyone hears of it is a complaint. A one-line check on the range of monthly would have stopped the batch. The contract A data contract is an agreement between the team that produces a table and the teams that consume it. Write it down as data, so code can enforce it and people can review it. Copy Validating a batch Copy What you should see Copy Copy Each failure says what broke in words an on-call engineer can act on. The new region is a good example of a contract doing its job: it is not necessarily wrong data, but a change the model was never trained on, and someone should decide what to do before it is scored. Distribution checks against a reference Range checks miss slower problems: values that stay legal but shift. Compare each batch with the training data. A two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic works for numeric columns; lesson 32.11 adds the population stability index used in monitoring. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Where validation runs Point Fail means Typical action Before training The pipeline stops; no new model version Fix the data or the contract, rerun Before batch scoring Scores are not published Keep yesterday's scores, alert the data owner Online, per request The request is rejected or flagged Return a safe default and log it Libraries such as Great Expectations, pandera and Soda implement the same idea with more checks and reports; in Snowflake, data metric functions run similar checks inside the warehouse. Start with a contract this small and grow it from real incidents. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A contract written as data can be enforced by code and reviewed by people. ✗ If every value is inside its allowed range, the batch is safe to score. Legal values can still shift in distribution; compare with a reference too. ✓ When scoring is blocked, keeping the previous scores is usually safer than publishing bad ones. Recap What to keep Contract: schema, types, ranges, allowed values, nulls, uniqueness, volume. Block, warn or pass, with messages a person can act on. Validate before training and before scoring; add distribution checks for slow shifts. Exercises Add a freshness rule: the newest updated_at must be less than 26 hours old. Make the KS threshold depend on sample size. Why does a fixed threshold misbehave for very large batches? Write the message the validator should post to the data owner's channel for the pence incident. a3206: Course home / Phase 32 · MLOps and LLMOps in Production Feature Pipelines: Point-in-Time Correctness, Leakage and Training-Serving Skew Lesson 32.6 60 min Lesson Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Build training data with point-in-time joins, so no feature uses information from after the prediction time Show how a naive join leaks the future and inflates offline scores Remove training-serving skew by computing features with one shared function Before you start Needs : Lesson 2.27 · Training-Serving Skew and Feature Stores ; Lesson 2.19 · Scikit-learn ML Pipelines Type : Lesson (build). Time : about an hour. In plain words first The idea in one line Each training row must only see what was known at the moment the prediction would have been made, and serving must compute features exactly the same way. The problem Lakeside's second churn model scored a superb AUC offline and was close to useless in production. The cause was one join: "number of support tickets" came from a table that included tickets raised after the customer had already called to cancel. The model had learned to spot cancellation calls, not churn risk. A spine and a feature table The spine lists the moments you want predictions for: one row per customer and prediction date, with the label observed later. The feature table holds values with the time they became known. Copy What you should see Copy Copy The naive join and the point-in-time join Copy What you should see Copy Copy The naive number is the one that gets a model approved and then fails. The point-in-time number is what production will actually see. Any feature built from events needs the event time and the prediction time in the join; feature stores (Feast, Snowflake Feature Store, Databricks) exist largely to do this join correctly at scale. In Snowflake's Feature Store, generate_training_set(spine_df, features, spine_timestamp_col=...) performs it (lesson 32.14 ). One feature function for training and serving Training-serving skew happens when the training pipeline (SQL in the warehouse) and the serving code (Python in an API) compute "the same" feature differently: different windows, null handling or rounding. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Three of the four features differ on this one request, and the fourth would differ as soon as a tenure value is missing. None of these raises an error. The fix is organisational as much as technical: one feature definition, versioned, used by both paths, with a test that feeds the same input through both and compares (lesson 32.8 ). Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A point-in-time join only uses feature values known at the prediction time. ✗ A higher offline AUC always means a better model. Leakage raises offline scores and hurts production; check how features were joined. ✓ Computing features with one shared function removes a whole class of training-serving skew. Recap What to keep Spine with prediction times; features with event times; join as of the prediction time. Suspiciously good offline scores are a leakage alarm. One feature definition for training and serving, tested for parity. Exercises Change the window to 30 days. How does the point-in-time AUC change, and why? Add a second as-of date per customer (2026-03-01) to the spine and rebuild the training set. Write a parity test that fails if the two feature functions differ by more than 1e-9 on 1,000 random requests. a3207: Course home / Phase 32 · MLOps and LLMOps in Production Training Pipelines and Orchestration: DAGs, Idempotent Steps, Caching and Backfills Lesson 32.7 60 min Lesson Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Express training as a pipeline of small steps with declared inputs and outputs Make steps idempotent and cache them by the hash of their inputs, so reruns are cheap and safe Run a backfill and explain how an orchestrator such as Airflow, Prefect, Kubeflow or Snowflake tasks schedules the same graph Before you start Needs : Lesson 10.19 · An End-to-End LLM Pipeline ; Lesson 2.19 · Scikit-learn ML Pipelines Type : Lesson (build). Time : about an hour. In plain words first The idea in one line Turn the notebook into a graph of steps that each do one thing, can be rerun safely, and skip work they have already done. The problem Level 1 maturity means the training pipeline runs without a person. That needs three properties a notebook lacks: steps that can run in order on a schedule, steps that give the same result when rerun (so a retry after a failure does no harm), and a record of what each run produced. A tiny orchestrator Real orchestrators add scheduling, retries, distribution and a UI, but the core is this: a graph of steps, each run with its inputs, its output cached under a key built from those inputs. Copy What you should see Copy Copy The rerun does no work: every step's inputs are unchanged, so every output comes from the cache. Changing C reruns only train and evaluate . This is what makes pipelines cheap to iterate on and safe to retry. Idempotence A step is idempotent if running it twice leaves the world as running it once. Reading and computing are naturally idempotent; writing needs care. Not idempotent Idempotent version INSERT INTO scores SELECT ... MERGE on (customer, score_date), or overwrite the partition for that date Append a model file named model_latest.pkl Write model/{run_id}/ and move an alias Send an alert email from inside training Write a status row; a separate notifier sends once Backfills A backfill reruns the pipeline for past dates, for example after fixing a feature bug. With date-parameterised, cached, idempotent steps it is a loop. Copy What you should see Copy Copy The same graph in a real orchestrator Copy In Snowflake, the same graph can be a set of tasks ( CREATE TASK ... AFTER ... ) calling stored procedures, or Snowflake ML Jobs for Python training code; on Kubernetes, Kubeflow Pipelines or Argo. The choice matters less than the properties: declared inputs, idempotent outputs, recorded runs. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Caching a step by the hash of its inputs and parameters lets a rerun skip unchanged work. ✗ INSERT INTO scores SELECT ... is idempotent because it always inserts the same rows. Running it twice inserts the rows twice; use MERGE or overwrite the date's partition. ✓ Date-parameterised steps make a backfill a loop over dates. Recap What to keep Small steps, declared inputs and outputs, a graph. Idempotent writes; cache by input hash. Backfills are loops; orchestrators add schedules, retries and history. Exercises Make validate fail for one date and show that downstream steps do not run for it. Add a register step that only runs when the evaluation beats 0.75 AUC. Rewrite the pipeline as Snowflake tasks in SQL (one task per step, AFTER dependencies), as text. a3208: Course home / Phase 32 · MLOps and LLMOps in Production Testing ML Systems and CI/CD for Models: Data, Feature, Model and Behavioural Tests Lesson 32.8 70 min Lesson Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Write the four kinds of ML tests: data, feature code, model quality and model behaviour Use invariance and directional tests to catch models that score well but behave badly Wire the tests into a CI workflow that blocks a release Before you start Needs : Lesson 2.13 · Model Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy, Precision, Recall and More ; Lesson 11.19 · Testing and Evaluating LLM Applications Type : Lesson (build). Time : about 70 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Test the data, the code and the model's behaviour automatically on every change, and let failing tests stop the release. The problem Ordinary software tests check code. A model can pass every code test and still be wrong: trained on bad data, worse on a slice, or relying on a feature it should not use. The ML Test Score rubric groups the extra tests into data, model development, infrastructure and monitoring. This lesson builds the first two and puts them in CI. Setup: a model and the shared feature function Copy The tests Copy What you should see Copy Copy The invariance test passes trivially here because features never reads gender . That is the point: the test protects you on the day someone adds it, or adds a feature that stands in for it, such as a title field. Breaking it on purpose Copy What you should see Copy Copy No exception, plausible output, and a quality test that catches it. Without the test, this ships. Wiring it into CI Copy Keep the CI training run small and fixed (a sampled snapshot) so it takes minutes, and run the full training in the pipeline after merge. Store the thresholds in the repository so that changing them is itself a reviewed change. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Invariance tests check that changing an attribute that should not matter leaves predictions unchanged. ✗ If the code tests pass, the model is ready to release. Data, quality-by-slice and behaviour tests are needed too. ✓ Thresholds kept in the repository make loosening a test a reviewed change. Recap What to keep Data tests, feature-code tests, quality by slice, behaviour tests. Invariance, directional and minimum-functionality cases catch silent failures. CI runs fast tests on every change and a small fixed training run before the gate. Exercises Add a directional test: a longer tenure should not raise risk. Does the model pass? Add a calibration test: in each tenth of predicted risk, the observed churn rate is within 5 points of the mean prediction. Turn the checks above into pytest functions in a tests/model file (as text), each with one assert. a3209: Course home / Phase 32 · MLOps and LLMOps in Production Packaging and Serving Models: Batch or Online, ONNX Export, Input Checks and Latency Budgets Lesson 32.9 65 min Lesson Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Choose between batch scoring and an online endpoint from the business need, not habit Export a scikit-learn pipeline to ONNX and prove the exported model gives the same answers Put input validation and a latency budget around an online model Before you start Needs : Lesson 0.17 · Docker Containers for AI Workloads ; Lesson 17.8 · LLM Inference Metrics: TTFT, TPOT, ITL, Goodput and P99 Latency Type : Lesson (build). Time : about 65 minutes. Setup : pip install skl2onnx onnxruntime for the export section. In plain words first The idea in one line Serve predictions in the simplest way that meets the deadline the business has, package the model so it runs the same everywhere, and guard the endpoint against bad inputs and slow answers. The problem Lakeside's platform team assumed the churn model needed a real-time API. The retention team only calls customers the next morning. A nightly batch job writing scores to a table would have been cheaper, simpler to monitor and easier to roll back. Batch or online Question Batch scoring Online endpoint When is the prediction needed? Hours later (campaigns, reports, queues) During a user interaction Inputs available All in the warehouse Some only at request time Cost Compute once per period Always-on service Failure handling Keep yesterday's scores Fallback answer needed in milliseconds Monitoring Compare full runs Per-request logs and sampling Lakeside chooses batch for the retention list, and online for one place: the cancellation page, where an offer must be chosen while the customer waits. A pipeline that travels: export to ONNX ONNX is a portable model format with fast runtimes for many languages and platforms. Exporting the whole scikit-learn pipeline (scaling included) avoids re-implementing preprocessing in the serving language. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Parity: prove the export is the same model Copy What you should see Copy Copy Run this parity test in CI for every exported version. Small floating-point differences are normal (ONNX computes in 32-bit floats); a large one means an unsupported option or a preprocessing step that did not export. Latency: measure percentiles, not averages Copy What you should see Copy Copy For one-row requests the runtime overhead dominates, and the ONNX runtime is usually several times faster than calling scikit-learn directly. The numbers on your machine will differ; what matters is that you measure p95 and p99 against the budget the product sets (for the cancellation page, say 50 ms for the whole request, of which the model may use 5). The endpoint: validate, predict, fall back Copy What you should see Copy Copy In production this function sits behind a web framework (FastAPI is common), runs in a container, and logs every request with the model version, inputs, output, latency and reason. Those logs are what monitoring (lesson 32.11 ) reads. Copy Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ If predictions are only used the next morning, batch scoring is usually the better design. ✗ An exported ONNX model can be trusted without testing because the converter is deterministic. Run a parity test on real inputs for every exported version. ✓ Latency budgets should be checked against p95 or p99, not the average. Recap What to keep Pick batch or online from when the prediction is needed. Export the whole pipeline; prove parity on real inputs. Validate inputs, measure percentiles, and always have a fallback. Three layers, from fastest to most trustworthy: Layer Available Tells you Input drift Immediately The world the model sees has changed Prediction drift Immediately The model's behaviour has changed Performance When labels arrive (churn: 30 to 60 days) Whether the model is still right Twelve weeks of scoring Copy What you should see Copy Copy The population stability index PSI compares the share of rows in each bin of a reference distribution with the share in the current one: the sum over bins of (current − reference) × ln(current / reference). Common rules of thumb: below 0.1 stable, 0.1 to 0.25 worth a look, above 0.25 a real shift. They are conventions, not laws; calibrate them on your own history. Copy What you should see Copy Copy The price rise shows up in monthly from week 6 and the outage in tickets from week 9; tenure stays flat. Copy What you should see Copy Copy AUC barely moves. Triggers Trigger Pros Cons Schedule (weekly, monthly) Simple, predictable Retrains when nothing changed; may be too slow after a shock Input or prediction drift Reacts early Drift does not always hurt performance Performance or calibration drop Retrains when it matters Waits for labels New data volume Uses data when there is enough of it Ignores whether anything changed Most teams combine a schedule with a performance trigger, and treat drift as a reason to look. A retraining loop with a gate Copy What you should see Copy Copy The trigger fires when the first post-change cohort matures (week 12), and the challenger wins on the held-out week. That model was trained on weeks 3 to 6, mostly from before the change, so a smaller gap remains; the trigger fires again at week 17, and the retrain on weeks 8 to 11, all after the change, closes it. After that the loop keeps the model and spends no more compute. The challenger is trained on weeks that exclude the holdout, and only after it wins is the final model refit on all matured weeks. Two design choices to notice: the window (recent weeks only) lets the model forget the old price relationship, at the cost of less data; and the gate stops a bad batch from replacing a good model automatically. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Observed churn drops at the threshold even though true risk keeps rising. Remedies: keep a small random holdout group that never receives offers and train on it (or weight it), record the action taken as a feature, or model the uplift of the offer directly rather than the risk. a3215: Course home / Phase 32 · MLOps and LLMOps in Production LLMOps: What Changes When the Model Is an API, and the Release Manifest That Tames It Lesson 32.15 55 min Lesson Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do List the artifacts that define an LLM application's behaviour and version them together Write a release manifest and diff two releases to decide which checks must run Explain how vendor model updates, non-determinism and per-request cost change operations Before you start Needs : Lesson 11.19 · Testing and Evaluating LLM Applications ; Lesson 17.13 · Choosing an LLM Observability Stack ; Lesson 17.19 · LiteLLM, Portkey, Kong and Bifrost: AI Gateways Type : Lesson (concepts with code). Time : about 55 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line An LLM application's behaviour is set by many small artifacts (prompts, model ID, settings, retrieval index, tools, guardrails); release them together as one versioned manifest, and test according to what changed. The problem Lakeside's support assistant drafts replies to customer emails. In one week, four people changed it: a product manager edited the system prompt, an engineer switched to a newer model version, the knowledge base was re-indexed after a policy update, and someone raised the temperature "to sound friendlier". Replies got worse. Nobody could say which change did it, because none of them was a "deployment". What defines behaviour Artifact Example Changes how often Model identifier claude-sonnet-5-5 When the vendor releases or retires models Generation settings temperature, max tokens, effort Occasionally Prompts system prompt, templates, few-shot examples Often Retrieval index version, embedding model, chunking, top-k Whenever documents change Tools tool names, schemas, descriptions With features Guardrails input and output filters, redaction rules With incidents and policy Eval set golden cases and graders Grows over time In classic ML, the weights are the artifact. In an LLM application the weights belong to someone else and these artifacts are the "model". So they get the same treatment: version control, review, testing and staged release. The release manifest Copy What you should see Copy Copy What changed decides what to test Copy What you should see Copy Copy Three changes in one release make a regression hard to attribute. The usual rule: change one artifact per release unless the changes are coupled (a new tool and the prompt that explains it). The manifest makes that rule checkable. Three operational differences from classic ML The vendor changes the model. Model versions are retired on a published schedule, and a pinned model identifier is the only protection from silent changes. Treat a model upgrade as a release with the heaviest test plan (lesson 32.19 ). Outputs vary. At temperature above zero the same input gives different outputs, and even at zero small variations can occur. Evaluate with several samples per case where consistency matters, and compare releases on many cases rather than reading single outputs. Every request costs money. Cost per request is an operational metric next to latency and errors. Prompt length, retrieval top-k and output length are cost levers; a prompt edit that adds 2,000 tokens is a cost change and should show up in review (Phase 17 covers caching, batching and routing). a3217: Course home / Phase 32 · MLOps and LLMOps in Production Evaluation Data from Production: Trace Sampling, Labelling Queues and Calibrated Judges Lesson 32.17 65 min Lesson Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Sample production traces for review so that rare failures are not drowned out by easy cases Grow a versioned golden set from reviewed traces Calibrate a model-based judge against human labels with Cohen's kappa before trusting it Before you start Needs : Lesson 11.19 · Testing and Evaluating LLM Applications ; Lesson 13.24 · End-to-End Tool-Call Tracing with OpenTelemetry GenAI ; Lesson 31.13 · Evals as the Contract: Golden Sets, Graders and a Release Gate Type : Lesson (build). Time : about 65 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Production traffic is the best source of test cases: sample it cleverly, have people label it, keep the best cases forever, and only let a model grade when it agrees with people. The problem Lakeside's golden set was written before launch from what the team imagined customers would ask. Three months in, customers ask about things nobody imagined, and the golden set no longer predicts how releases will do. The fix is a loop: traces in, review, golden set out. Sampling traces for review Uniform sampling mostly picks easy cases. Stratify by slice and over-sample signals of trouble: a thumbs-down, a long conversation, a guardrail flag, a low retrieval score. Copy What you should see Copy Copy The weighted sample finds several times more failures for the same reviewing effort and gives rare topics such as cancellations a fair share. Its failure rate is not the production failure rate, though: to estimate that, use the uniform sample or re-weight. From reviewed traces to a golden set Copy What you should see Copy Copy Keep a few passing cases too, so the set does not become a museum of failures that any change seems to "improve". Freeze each version; scores are only comparable on the same version. Calibrating a model judge People cannot label every release. A model judge (an LLM grading replies against a rubric) can, if it agrees with people. Measure agreement on a sample both have labelled, with Cohen's kappa, which corrects for agreement by chance. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Raw agreement flatters the lenient judge because most replies pass. Its kappa of 0.62 even clears a common rule-of-thumb bar, yet it catches only about half of the failures people found. That is why the bar has two parts: kappa of about 0.6 or more and high recall on the failure class, before the judge gates releases, with a fresh human sample each month to check it has not drifted. Weighting changes the mix; use a uniform sample or re-weight to estimate rates. ✓ Cohen's kappa corrects agreement for chance, which matters when most cases pass. In plain words first The idea in one line You rarely know whether an LLM answer was right, so watch the signals that move when it is not, and watch what people are asking, because that is what drifts. The problem Lesson 32.11 monitored a model whose labels arrive in six weeks. An LLM reply has no label at all unless someone reviews it. Lakeside needs signals available on every request, and alerts that point at a cause. Signal What it suggests Caveat Thumbs-down rate Users dislike replies Few users vote; voters are unhappy more often Edit distance of agent edits Drafts need rework Only where a person edits before sending Escalation or reopen rate The reply did not solve it Lagging by days Guardrail flag rate Policy risk in inputs or outputs Depends on filter versions Refusal rate Over-cautious prompts or model change Some refusals are right Cost per request, tokens Prompt or retrieval growth Moves with traffic mix p95 latency Slow model, long outputs, tool timeouts Vendor-side variance Topic mix Users ask about new things Needs a topic classifier Six weeks of request logs Copy What you should see Copy Copy The weekly report Copy What you should see Copy Copy Two changes stand out. Cost per thousand requests jumps in week 4 with no change in quality: the longer prompt shipped. Thumbs-down and edit lengths rise in week 5. The weekly numbers alone do not say why. Topic drift explains the quality drop Copy What you should see Copy Copy From week 5 the share of "other" questions jumps (customers asking about the new tariff), and that topic carries most of the thumbs-downs. The knowledge base and golden set do not cover the tariff. The action is not "retrain"; it is: add the tariff documents to the index, add tariff cases to the golden set (lesson 32.17 ), and release through the gate. a3219: Course home / Phase 32 · MLOps and LLMOps in Production Model Upgrades and Adapters: Migrating to a New Model Version and Serving Fine-Tuned LoRA Adapters Lesson 32.19 60 min Lesson Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Plan a model migration before the vendor retires the current version Decide a migration with paired results by slice, plus cost and latency, rather than a single average Explain how fine-tuned LoRA adapters are versioned and served next to a shared base model Before you start Needs : Lesson 17.28 · Choosing a Self-Hosted Serving Engine for Your Hardware and Scale ; Lesson 17.9 · Quantization in Production: AWQ, GPTQ, GGUF K-Quants, FP8 and MXFP4/NVFP4 ; Lesson 17.20 · Progressive Deployment for LLMs: Shadow Traffic and Canary Rollouts Type : Lesson (build). Time : about an hour. In plain words first The idea in one line A new model version is the biggest change an LLM application gets; test it like a new model, slice by slice, and plan it before the old one is retired. The problem Every hosted model has a retirement date. Teams that pin a model (as they should) eventually must move, often under time pressure. Lakeside's assistant runs on a model that is scheduled for deprecation; a newer, cheaper one is available. Is it safe to switch? A migration report on the golden set The golden set (lesson 32.17 ) is run on both models. Results are paired : the same case, two models. That allows a precise comparison and shows where they disagree. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Read it slice by slice. The new model is clearly cheaper and faster, but the overall interval spans zero: on quality it is not shown to be better or worse. It gains on tariff and technical questions and drops on billing and cancellations. With 84 and 32 cases those drops may be noise, but they are the customers who matter most for revenue, so read every one of the 24 cases it breaks before deciding. A typical decision: migrate, with a prompt fix for the weak slices verified by the gate, and keep the old model available as a fallback until the retirement date. The migration plan When Step On the announcement Add the new model to the eval matrix; run the golden set; estimate cost Before switching Fix prompts for weak slices; rerun; shadow traffic for a few days (lesson 32.10 ) Switch Canary by percentage; guardrails on thumbs-down, refusals, latency, cost After Keep the old model ID as a fallback until it is retired; update the release manifest Fine-tuned adapters Some teams fine-tune an open-weight model for a narrow task. LoRA trains small low-rank matrices instead of all weights, so each fine-tune is a small adapter file over a shared base model. Operationally, an adapter is a model version: it needs a registry entry, the base model it was trained for, its training data fingerprint, eval results and an alias. Several adapters can be served from one copy of the base model. Copy Copy What you should see Copy Copy An adapter only works with the base model it was trained on; upgrading the base model means retraining and re-evaluating every adapter. Keep that dependency in the registry so the check is automatic. Set --max-lora-rank to the largest rank among your adapters, as the vLLM docs advise, and do not enable runtime adapter loading in production: the docs flag it as a security risk. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Paired results on the same golden cases give a sharper comparison than two separate averages. ✗ If the new model is better on average, it can be switched in without looking at slices. A slice can get worse while the average improves; read the cases it breaks. ✓ A LoRA adapter must be re-evaluated when the base model changes. Recap What to keep Plan migrations from the announcement, not the retirement date. Paired results, slices, broken cases, cost and latency; then shadow and canary. Adapters are model versions tied to a base model; register that dependency. Exercises Raise the cancel slice's new pass rate to 0.9 and rerun. What changes in the decision? Compute the monthly saving at 40,000 requests a day, and the number of broken cases you would accept for it. Add training_data and eval_set fields to the adapter registry, and block promotion if the eval set version is older than the production adapter's.
